reason: The sources support a surprising story with ample verified claims and visual options.
story: Discovered in October 2005, the exoplanet HD 189733 b is located roughly 64 light-years away in the constellation Vulpecula. Orbiting its star in just 2.2 days, this gas giant is tidally locked, featuring a scorching day side and a cooler night side. Driven by extreme temperature differences, howling winds roar across the planet at speeds up to 5,400 miles per hour. These supersonic gales carry vaporized silicate particles from the day side to the night side, where they condense into liquid droplets. The result is a bizarre and terrifying weather system: molten glass raining sideways across the planet. Despite appearing as a deep blue dot from space due to its hazy silicate-laced atmosphere, this hellish hot Jupiter offers zero prospects for life, complete with extreme heat and newly detected hydrogen sulfide.
angle: A deep-blue alien world where winds blow at 5,400 mph and drive horizontal storms of molten glass rain.

claims.claim: HD 189733 b was discovered on October 5, 2005.
The exoplanet is located approximately 64 to 64.5 light-years away from the Solar System in the constellation Vulpecula.
HD 189733 b completes one orbit around its host star every 2.2 days.
The planet belongs to a class of planets called hot Jupiters.
HD 189733 b is tidally locked, meaning one side always faces the star and the other is always dark.
Winds on HD 189733 b reach speeds of up to 5,400 miles per hour.
The planet's weather includes raining molten glass or silicate droplets.
The glass rain is blown sideways by the extreme winds.
When viewed from space, the planet appears as a deep blue dot.
The blue color is caused by Rayleigh scattering from silicate particles and haze in its atmosphere rather than an ocean.
NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope measured infrared light to create one of the first temperature maps for an exoplanet.
Hydrogen sulfide was detected in the atmosphere of HD 189733 b.

disputed: Exact day side temperature figures vary slightly across sources (e.g., ~1,700°F to nearly 3,700°F, or 1340 to 1540 K); scripts should state 'temperatures soaring into the thousands of degrees'.
